title: A secret letter, written out of fear for family.
subtitle: Hatib's mistake, and the Prophet's ﷺ mercy
then: Hatib, an early emigrant who fought at Badr, had family in Makkah with no tribe to protect them. Before the march on Makkah, he {trap}secretly wrote to the Quraysh{/trap} to earn their favour. Allah informed the Prophet ﷺ and the letter was retrieved. Hatib said he did it out of fear, not disbelief. The Prophet ﷺ said, {reward}he has told you the truth{/reward}, and mentioned that he had been at Badr.
now: You bend a rule at work to protect your kids' future. You share something you were trusted to keep, just to stay on good terms with someone powerful. {trap}Fear for family can make good people do disloyal things.{/trap} {idea}Allah sees the hidden motive, and the Prophet ﷺ still met Hatib with mercy.{/idea}
old: If I do it to protect my family, it cannot be wrong.
new: Even love for family can lead me astray. Allah sees my reasons, and mercy is still open.
try: Think of one thing you are doing out of fear for family. Ask if Allah would approve of it.

title: The favour you are buying will not be returned.
subtitle: What they wanted for you all along

picture.label: If they had the upper hand

row.title: their real wish
sub: that I give up my faith

then: Hatib hoped his letter would make the Quraysh indebted to him. The verse explains why that hope was misplaced: {trap}if they gained the upper hand, they would be enemies{/trap}, using hands and tongues against the believers. {idea}What they truly wanted was for them to disbelieve.{/idea}
now: The coworker you keep flattering, hoping they will speak up for you in the meeting. They have already shown they want you out. {idea}Some goodwill cannot be bought,{/idea} and trying only costs you your integrity.
old: If I keep doing favours for people who dislike me, they will protect me.
new: Some people want me to lose my faith. Favours will not change that.
try: Stop one small thing you do only to win over someone who wishes you harm.

title: The relatives you risked it for cannot help you then.
subtitle: On the Day, each stands alone
then: Hatib's whole motive was his relatives and children in Makkah. This verse speaks to that directly: {trap}neither your relatives nor your children will benefit you{/trap} on the Day of Resurrection. {idea}He will judge between you, and He sees what you do.{/idea}
now: You cut a corner for your family's sake: the forged signature, the white lie on the form. On the Day, they will not be standing between you and the question. {idea}Love them, but do not sin for them.{/idea}
old: Doing wrong for my family is a kind of sacrifice.
new: My family cannot answer for me. I should never disobey Allah for their sake.
try: Do one good thing for your family today that is fully halal and honest.

title: Ibrahim stood apart from what his people worshipped.
subtitle: An excellent example, with one exception
then: After Hatib's story, the surah offers a model: {idea}Ibrahim and those with him{/idea}, who told their people they disowned the idols until they believed in Allah alone. Ibn Kathir notes the exception: Ibrahim's promise to seek forgiveness for his father is not an example to copy. Then they turned to Allah: {reward}in You we trust, to You we turn.{/reward}
now: Everyone at the office party is doing something you do not do. You are the only one holding a juice. It feels lonely. {idea}Ibrahim stood alone against his whole people,{/idea} and the first thing he did after was turn to Allah in trust.
old: Standing apart from the crowd means I will be alone.
new: Standing for my faith like Ibrahim means leaning fully on Allah.
try: Say Ibrahim's dua today: Rabbana alayka tawakkalna wa ilayka anabna wa ilayka al-masir.

title: Do not make us a reason for others to doubt.
subtitle: Ibrahim's prayer about being a trial

row.title: they lost, so they are wrong

then: Mujahid explained the prayer: do not let us be punished, {trap}or they will say, had these people been on the truth, this would not have struck them.{/trap} Ibn Kathir explains forgive us as {reward}cover our mistakes from being exposed to others, and forgive what is between us and You.{/reward}
now: You are the one Muslim your coworkers know well. When you lose your temper, they do not just judge you, they judge your faith. {idea}This dua asks Allah to keep your flaws from turning people away from the truth.{/idea}
new: My failings can make others doubt the truth, so I ask Allah to cover and forgive them.
try: Say this dua today: Rabbana la taj'alna fitnatan lilladhina kafaru waghfir lana.

title: The example is for those who hope to meet Allah.
subtitle: Why Ibrahim's way speaks to you
then: The verse repeats that Ibrahim and his people are an excellent pattern, {reward}for those who look forward to Allah and the Last Day.{/reward} Ibn Kathir says it encourages believers in the Return. Whoever turns away, {idea}Allah is the perfectly Rich, the Praiseworthy.{/idea}
now: Your role models are mostly people from your feed: fitness, money, travel. They tell you how to look and earn. {idea}Ibrahim's example is for the person who is hoping to meet Allah.{/idea} Which hope is shaping your choices?
old: Role models are people who succeeded in this world.
new: If my hope is in meeting Allah, Ibrahim is the model to follow.
try: Read one story of Ibrahim in the Quran this week, starting today.

title: Today's enemy may be tomorrow's dear friend.
subtitle: Allah can turn hostility into love
then: Ibn Kathir says this means {reward}affection after animosity, tenderness after coldness{/reward}, as Allah did for the Ansar who had been enemies before He joined their hearts. He cites the hadith: {idea}love your loved one moderately, he may become your enemy; hate moderately, he may become your beloved one day.{/idea}
now: The in-law you have not spoken to in two years. The old friend who betrayed you. You have decided this is permanent. {idea}Allah is able to bring hearts together{/idea} in ways you cannot plan. Leave the door slightly open.
old: Once someone becomes my enemy, that never changes.
new: Allah can turn enmity into love, so I should not hate beyond measure.
try: Make dua today for one person you are estranged from, that Allah softens both your hearts.

title: Be kind and fair to those who do not fight your faith.
subtitle: Asma's mother came with gifts

row.title: keep away from all
sub: who do not share my faith

then: Asma bint Abi Bakr's mother, not yet Muslim, came visiting with gifts during the truce. Asma {trap}refused the gifts and would not let her in.{/trap} The verse came, and the Prophet ﷺ told her to accept the gifts and let her in. {reward}Keep good relations with your mother.{/reward}
now: Your neighbour of a different faith brings over food at Christmas. Your non-Muslim aunt calls on Eid. {reward}This verse is your answer: be kind, be fair.{/reward} Allah loves those who deal justly.
old: I should keep my distance from people who do not share my faith.
new: Kindness and fairness to people of any faith who mean me no harm is something Allah loves.
try: Do one kind thing today for a neighbour or relative of a different faith.

title: The line is drawn at those who fought your faith.
subtitle: Kindness is wide, alliance has limits

row.title: kindness
sub: to those who mean no harm

then: Right after permitting kindness, the verse names the limit precisely: those who {trap}fought the believers because of religion and drove them from their homes{/trap}, like the Quraysh of that time. Ibn Kathir explains these were the openly hostile, and allying with them is wrongdoing. {idea}The restriction is narrow and specific.{/idea}
now: Not everyone who differs from you is against you. But someone who mocks your prayer, pressures you to drop your faith, and works to push you out is different. {idea}You can be polite, but you do not hand them your loyalty.{/idea}
old: Either I treat everyone as a friend, or everyone as a threat.
new: Kindness is wide, but I do not give my loyalty to those who wage war on my faith.
try: Notice one relationship that pulls you away from your faith, and set one gentle boundary.

title: Allah knows best who truly believes.
subtitle: The women who emigrated after Hudaybiyyah

row.title: Allah knows best
sub: we judge only what is shown

then: After the Hudaybiyyah treaty, Umm Kulthum bint Uqbah {reward}emigrated to Madinah{/reward}, and her brothers came to take her back. The verse said believing women were not to be returned. Their test, Ibn Abbas said, was the testimony of faith, yet the verse reminds: {idea}Allah knows best about their faith.{/idea}
now: The new revert at the mosque who does not pray the way you do. The sister who started wearing hijab last month. You might wonder if they are sincere. {idea}Allah knows best what is in their hearts.{/idea} Welcome what you see.
old: I can tell who is really sincere in their faith.
new: Only Allah knows a heart. I accept what people show and leave the rest to Him.
try: Welcome someone newer to the faith today with warmth, not questions.

title: Even in separation, settle what is owed fairly.
subtitle: Fair dealing when marriages ended

row.title: it is over, so anything goes

then: Ibn Kathir explains that as marriages between the two sides ended, Allah ordered the dowries to be {reward}returned to the husbands who had paid them{/reward}, on both sides. If a Muslim's wife went over and nothing was returned, he was to be paid the equivalent. The verse closes: {idea}fear Allah, in whom you believe.{/idea}
now: The divorce papers, the business partnership falling apart, the flatmate moving out. It is tempting to grab what you can because the relationship is over. {idea}The verse says: settle fairly, even now.{/idea}
old: Once a relationship ends, I can just protect my own interests.
new: Even when things end, I still owe fairness, because I fear Allah.
try: If you owe anything to someone you have parted ways with, settle it this week.

title: The women's pledge, as much as you are able.
subtitle: Promises made directly to the Prophet ﷺ

row.title: as much as you can bear

then: Aishah said the Prophet ﷺ accepted women's pledges with words alone, saying {idea}I have accepted your pledge.{/idea} Umaymah bint Ruqayqah said he added: {reward}as much as you are able and can bear.{/reward} The women replied, Allah and His Messenger are more merciful to us than we are to ourselves.
now: You read a list like this and feel crushed: I will never be perfect. The Prophet ﷺ answered that feeling in advance. {reward}As much as you can.{/reward} Then he was told to ask forgiveness for them, because Allah is Forgiving.
old: If I cannot keep every promise to Allah perfectly, there is no point.
new: Allah asks for my sincere best, and forgiveness covers the gap.
try: Renew one promise to Allah today and add: as much as I am able.

title: Do not lean on those who lost hope in the Hereafter.
subtitle: The surah ends where it began
then: The surah closes as it opened, warning against close alliance with those under Allah's anger. Ibn Kathir gives two meanings for the despair: {trap}they do not expect to meet their buried relatives again{/trap}, since they deny the Resurrection, or {trap}like the dead disbeliever who sees his end and loses all hope.{/trap}
now: Your closest circle jokes that nothing comes after death, so get what you can now. You laugh along, and slowly your own hope fades. {idea}Who you lean on shapes what you hope for.{/idea} Keep some people near who remind you of the meeting with Allah.
old: Who I am close to does not affect my faith.
new: My closest companions shape my hope. I keep near those who look forward to the Hereafter.
try: Message one friend today who reminds you of Allah, and plan to see them.
